claim: Calmodulin (CaM) is a ubiquitously expressed EF-hand Ca2+-binding hub protein.
source: Calmodulin (CaM) is a ubiquitously expressed EF-hand Ca2+-binding hub protein, which regulates a plethora of Ca2+-dependent cellular processes such as ion transport, muscle contraction, proliferation, and apoptosis (Berchtold and Villalobo, 2014; Chin and Means, 2000; Villalobo et al., 2018; Villarroel et al., 2014; Yap et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on calmodulin.

claim: CaM regulates Ca2+-dependent cellular processes such as ion transport, muscle contraction, proliferation, and apoptosis.
source: Calmodulin (CaM) is a ubiquitously expressed EF-hand Ca2+-binding hub protein, which regulates a plethora of Ca2+-dependent cellular processes such as ion transport, muscle contraction, proliferation, and apoptosis (Berchtold and Villalobo, 2014; Chin and Means, 2000; Villalobo et al., 2018; Villarroel et al., 2014; Yap et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on CaM function.

claim: CaM is a small, α-helical protein consisting of two similar, but not identical, N- and C-terminal domains connected by a helical linker with a disordered, flexible hinge.
source: CaM is a small, α-helical protein consisting of two similar, but not identical, N- and C-terminal domains (for CaM termed the N-lobe and C-lobe, respectively) connected by a helical linker with a disordered, flexible hinge.
evidence: Describes the structural organization of CaM based on established knowledge.

claim: CaM binds up to four Ca2+ ions upon changes in free cytosolic Ca2+ concentration.
source: Upon changes in the free cytosolic Ca2+ concentration, [Ca2+]i, CaM binds up to four Ca2+ ions.
evidence: Established knowledge about CaM's Ca2+-binding capacity.

claim: Ca2+ binding to CaM induces structural rearrangements exposing hydrophobic patches through which CaM interacts with numerous structurally and functionally different proteins.
source: This induces structural rearrangements exposing hydrophobic patches through which CaM interacts with numerous structurally and functionally different proteins (Tidow and Nissen, 2013; Villalobo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations describing CaM's mechanism of protein interaction.

claim: In most cases studied to date, CaM wraps both its lobes around its α-helix-forming targets.
source: In most cases where this has been studied to date, CaM wraps both its lobes around its α-helix-forming targets, exemplified by the interaction with myosin light chain kinase (Ikura et al., 1992; Meador et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies of CaM-target interactions.

claim: Recent structures have shown diversity in CaM binding modes and motifs.
source: However, recent structures have shown diversity in binding and a range of CaM binding modes and motifs exist.
evidence: Refers to recent structural findings indicating diverse binding modes.

claim: In some cases, CaM with Ca2+ present only in one lobe is bound to the target.
source: Indeed, in some cases, CaM with Ca2+ present only in one lobe is bound to the target, whereas in other cases only the apo-form of CaM is bound (Lee et al., 2019; Nunomura et al., 2014; Nunomura et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing partial Ca2+ occupancy in CaM-target complexes.

claim: Common features of CaM-binding regions include high α-helix propensity, net positive charge, and obligate hydrophobic docking residues.
source: Still, common features of CaM-binding regions, such as high α-helix propensity, net positive charge, and obligate hydrophobic docking residues, exist (Villalobo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation describing common features of CaM-binding regions.

claim: CaM engages with many membrane proteins including estrogen receptor alfa (ERα), voltage-gated K+ channel Kv10.1 (eag1), and aquaporin 0.
source: CaM also engages with many membrane proteins and examples include the CaM substrates estrogen receptor alfa (ERα; Li et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2012), the voltage-gated K+ channel Kv10.1 (eag1; Schönherr et al., 2000; Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016), and aquaporin 0 (Reichow et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies of CaM interactions with specific membrane proteins.

claim: NHE1 (SLC9A1) is a major acid-extruding transporter localized in the plasma membrane in essentially all mammalian cells studied.
source: One widely studied CaM-binding membrane protein is the Na+/H+ exchanger, NHE1 (SLC9A1), a major acid-extruding transporter localized in the plasma membrane in essentially all mammalian cells studied (Orlowski and Grinstein, 2011; Pedersen and Counillon, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to reviews on NHE1 localization and function.

claim: Upon activation by cytosolic acidification or signaling events, NHE1 extrudes H+ from the cytosol in exchange for Na+ ions.
source: Upon activation by cytosolic acidification or a wide range of mitogenic and other signaling events, NHE1 extrudes H+ from the cytosol in exchange for Na+ ions.
evidence: Describes the functional mechanism of NHE1 based on established knowledge.

claim: NHE1 regulates key cellular functions such as proliferation, growth/death balance, cell volume, cell motility, and tissue homeostasis.
source: In addition to its role in intracellular pH (pHi) regulation, NHE1 regulates key cellular functions such as proliferation, growth/death balance, cell volume, cell motility, and tissue homeostasis (Orlowski and Grinstein, 2011; Pedersen and Counillon, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to reviews on NHE1 function.

claim: NHE1 hyperactivity is implicated in cancers, cardiovascular disease, ischemia-reperfusion damage, cardiac hypertrophy, and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis.
source: Consequently, NHE1 hyperactivity is implicated in many important pathologies including cancers (Cardone et al., 2005; Stock and Pedersen, 2017), as well as cardiovascular disease, especially ischemia-reperfusion damage and cardiac hypertrophy (Imahashi et al., 2007; Karmazyn et al., 1999; Nakamura et al., 2008) and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (Prasad et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies linking NHE1 to various pathologies.

claim: NHE1 functions as a dimer.
source: NHE1 which, like many other membrane transport proteins, functions as a dimer (Fafournoux et al., 1994; Pedersen and Counillon, 2019), consists of a 12-transmembrane (TM)-helix transport domain and an ~300 residue long cytoplasmic C-terminal domain with extensive disordered regions (Nørholm et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies demonstrating NHE1 dimerization.

claim: NHE1 consists of a 12-transmembrane helix transport domain and an ~300 residue long cytoplasmic C-terminal domain with extensive disordered regions.
source: NHE1 which, like many other membrane transport proteins, functions as a dimer (Fafournoux et al., 1994; Pedersen and Counillon, 2019), consists of a 12-transmembrane (TM)-helix transport domain and an ~300 residue long cytoplasmic C-terminal domain with extensive disordered regions (Nørholm et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to structural characterization of NHE1.

claim: NHE1 activity is regulated through multiple phosphorylation–dephosphorylation events and interactions with binding partners including CaM.
source: Via this tail, NHE1 activity is regulated through multiple phosphorylation–dephosphorylation events and interactions with a plethora of binding partners, one of which is CaM (for reviews, see Hendus-Altenburger et al., 2014; Orlowski and Grinstein, 2011; Pedersen and Counillon, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to reviews on NHE1 regulation.

claim: CaM binds directly to the cytoplasmic domain of NHE1 in the presence of Ca2+.
source: CaM binds directly to the cytoplasmic domain of NHE1 in the presence of Ca2+ (Bertrand et al., 1994; Köster et al., 2011) as originally demonstrated in vitro by binding of either an NHE1 fusion protein or full-length protein (Bertrand et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies demonstrating CaM-NHE1 binding.

claim: Binding of Ca2+-loaded CaM to NHE1 in response to an increase in [Ca2+]i elicits an alkaline shift in the pHi sensitivity of NHE1, resulting in its activation at less acidic pHi.
source: The binding of Ca2+-loaded CaM to NHE1 in response to an increase in [Ca2+]i elicits an alkaline shift in the pHi sensitivity of NHE1 in cells, resulting in its activation at less acidic pHi (Bertrand et al., 1994; Wakabayashi et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing functional effects of CaM binding to NHE1.

claim: NHE1:CaM interaction has been proposed to activate NHE1 by relieving an autoinhibitory interaction of the C-terminal tail of NHE1 with its TM region.
source: Mechanistically, NHE1:CaM interaction has been proposed to activate NHE1 by relieving an autoinhibitory interaction of the C-terminal tail of NHE1 with its TM region (Ikeda et al., 1997; Wakabayashi et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies proposing a mechanism for CaM-mediated NHE1 activation.

claim: CaM binding has been implicated in activation of NHE1 by hormones and growth factors including epidermal growth factor, serotonin, angiotensin, and endothelin.
source: CaM binding has also been implicated in activation of NHE1 by a wide range of hormones and growth factors, including epidermal growth factor, serotonin, angiotensin, and endothelin (Coaxum et al., 2009; Li et al., 2013; Turner et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies linking CaM to hormone/growth factor-mediated NHE1 activation.

claim: NHE1:CaM interaction was suggested to be regulated by Akt kinase-mediated phosphorylation of S648 of human NHE1.
source: NHE1:CaM interaction was suggested to be regulated by Akt kinase-mediated phosphorylation of S648 of human NHE1.
evidence: Refers to prior suggestions in the literature about S648 phosphorylation.

claim: The role of S648 phosphorylation in NHE1 regulation has been reported both as inhibitory and stimulatory.
source: However, the role of S648 phosphorylation in NHE1 regulation has been reported both as inhibitory (Snabaitis et al., 2008) and stimulatory (Meima et al., 2009), pointing to a possible context dependence of NHE1:CaM complex formation.
evidence: Supported by citations to conflicting reports on S648 phosphorylation effects.

claim: Two neighboring α-helical CaM-binding sites of NHE1 each bind CaM, but with different affinities.
source: Two neighboring α-helical CaM-binding sites of NHE1 each bind CaM, but with different affinities.
evidence: Refers to established knowledge about NHE1's CaM-binding sites.

claim: For an NHE1 variant deleted in CaM-binding region 2 (CB2, defined as D656-L691), Kd was ~20 nM.
source: For an NHE1 variant deleted in CaM-binding region 2 (CB2, defined as D656-L691), Kd was ~20 nM and for an NHE1 variant deleted in CaM-binding region 1 (CB1, defined as N637-A656) Kd was ~350 nM (Figure 1a, b, Bertrand et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study measuring binding affinities.

claim: For an NHE1 variant deleted in CaM-binding region 1 (CB1, defined as N637-A656), Kd was ~350 nM.
source: For an NHE1 variant deleted in CaM-binding region 2 (CB2, defined as D656-L691), Kd was ~20 nM and for an NHE1 variant deleted in CaM-binding region 1 (CB1, defined as N637-A656) Kd was ~350 nM (Figure 1a, b, Bertrand et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study measuring binding affinities.

claim: Deletion or mutation of CB1 resulted in loss of NHE1 [Ca2+]i responsiveness.
source: Testifying to its importance, deletion or mutation of CB1 resulted in loss of NHE1 [Ca2+]i responsiveness (Bertrand et al., 1994; Wakabayashi et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing functional effects of CB1 mutations.

claim: A crystal structure of CaM bound to a peptide of NHE1 containing both CaM-binding sites (A622-R690) revealed an unusual binding mode where CaM assumed an extended configuration.
source: A crystal structure of CaM bound to a peptide of NHE1 containing both CaM-binding sites (A622-R690) revealed an unusual binding mode. CaM assumed an extended configuration, and the N-terminal CaM-binding site of NHE1 (H1 in the following) made an uncommon interaction with the 'back side' of the C-lobe, whereas the N-lobe of CaM engaged with the low-affinity C-terminal site of NHE1 (H2 in the following) forming an α-helix in the hydrophobic ligand-binding groove (Köster et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to crystal structure study.

claim: In the crystal structure, the N-terminal CaM-binding site of NHE1 (H1) made an uncommon interaction with the 'back side' of the C-lobe of CaM.
source: CaM assumed an extended configuration, and the N-terminal CaM-binding site of NHE1 (H1 in the following) made an uncommon interaction with the 'back side' of the C-lobe, whereas the N-lobe of CaM engaged with the low-affinity C-terminal site of NHE1 (H2 in the following) forming an α-helix in the hydrophobic ligand-binding groove (Köster et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to crystal structure study.

claim: In the crystal structure, the N-lobe of CaM engaged with the low-affinity C-terminal site of NHE1 (H2) forming an α-helix in the hydrophobic ligand-binding groove.
source: CaM assumed an extended configuration, and the N-terminal CaM-binding site of NHE1 (H1 in the following) made an uncommon interaction with the 'back side' of the C-lobe, whereas the N-lobe of CaM engaged with the low-affinity C-terminal site of NHE1 (H2 in the following) forming an α-helix in the hydrophobic ligand-binding groove (Köster et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to crystal structure study.

claim: Small-angle X-ray scattering analysis of the CaM:NHE1 complex showed a poor fit to the crystal structure.
source: So far, the only analysis of the complex in solution was conducted using small-angle X-ray scattering (Köster et al., 2011). Here, the derived molecular envelope showed a poor fit to the crystal structure, further spurring a re-evaluation of the conformational landscape of the CaM:NHE1 complex to understand its functional relevance.
evidence: Supported by citation to SAXS study showing discrepancy with crystal structure.

claim: H1 (NHE1622-657) bound CaM with high affinity, with one CaM molecule binding two H1 peptides (n = 1.92 ± 0.06).
source: In line with previous results (Bertrand et al., 1994), H1 bound CaM with high affinity. In addition, we surprisingly observed that one CaM molecule bound two H1 peptides (n = 1.92 ± 0.06, Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by ITC data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Fitting the ITC data for H1:CaM to a binding model with two independent sites revealed similar high affinities (Kd,1 = 27 ± 8 nM; Kd,2 = 42 ± 6 nM).
source: Fitting the ITC data to a binding model with two independent sites revealed similar high affinities (Kd,1 = 27 ± 8 nM; Kd,2 = 42 ± 6 nM, Figure 1c), but with different enthalpic and entropic contributions (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by ITC data analysis shown in Figure 1c and Table 1.

claim: The affinity of H2 (NHE1651-692) for CaM was almost three magnitudes weaker (Kd = 9.0 ± 0.6 µM) than that of H1.
source: We then addressed the binding of the second helix, H2, to CaM. Here, the affinity was almost three magnitudes weaker (Kd = 9.0 ± 0.6 µM) than that of H1.
evidence: Supported by ITC data analysis.

claim: The H2:CaM interaction showed only one transition, indicating the formation of a 1:1 complex (n = 1.15 ± 0.08).
source: This interaction showed only one transition, indicating the formation of a 1:1 complex (n = 1.15 ± 0.08, Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by ITC data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The binding isotherm for the H1H2 peptide displayed two distinct transitions, suggesting successive binding events and/or diverse binding modes with different CaM:H1H2 stoichiometries.
source: Finally, the binding isotherm for the H1H2 peptide displayed two distinct transitions, suggesting successive binding events and/or diverse binding modes with different CaM:H1H2 stoichiometries.
evidence: Supported by ITC data analysis.

claim: Fitting H1H2:CaM ITC data to a two-site binding model gave Kd,1 = 0.27 ± 0.07 nM with stoichiometry n1 = 1.04 ± 0.05, and Kd,2 = 560 ± 15 nM with n2 = 1.22 ± 0.06.
source: Fitting to a two-site binding model allowed us to determine the affinity of the first binding event to Kd,1 = 0.27 ± 0.07 nM with a stoichiometry of 1 (n1 = 1.04 ± 0.05), and the affinity of the second binding event to Kd,2 = 560 ± 15 nM with n2 = 1.22 ± 0.06, summing up to a total stoichiometry of 1:2 (Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by ITC data analysis shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Upon addition of H1 to CaM at 1:1 ratio, most NMR signals from both CaM lobes broadened drastically, indicating exchange between free and bound state(s) on an intermediate NMR timescale.
source: Upon addition of H1 (50 µM CaM + 50 µM NHE1), most signals from both CaM lobes broadened drastically, indicating exchange between free and bound state(s) on an intermediate NMR timescale (kex ≈ Δδ) (Prestel et al., 2018; Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2b and citation to NMR methodology.

claim: After addition of excess H1 peptide (50 µM CaM + 125 µM H1, 1:2 ratio), the NMR signals re-sharpened and no further spectral changes were observed upon further addition of H1.
source: After addition of excess H1 peptide (50 µM CaM + 125 µM H1, denoted 1:2 in the following), the signals re-sharpened and no further spectral changes were observed upon further addition of H1 (Figure 2a, b).
evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2a, b.

claim: At a molar ratio of 1:1 (CaM:H1), signals from the C-lobe of CaM were located close to the position of the fully bound state (1:2), while signals of the N-lobe were positioned close to those of the free form of CaM.
source: Although at a molar ratio of 1:1 all the NMR signals were broadened by exchange processes, it was evident that signals from the C-lobe of CaM were located close to the position of the fully bound state (1:2), while signals of the N-lobe were positioned close to those of the free form of CaM, as exemplified for G135 and G62, respectively (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: At 1:1 stoichiometry (CaM:H1), H1 is bound to the higher affinity C-lobe in the main state.
source: This suggested that in the main state at a 1:1 stoichiometry H1 is bound to the higher affinity C-lobe, as depicted in the cartoon in Figure 2c.
evidence: Inferred from NMR data and depicted in Figure 2c.

claim: Large chemical shift perturbations were observed for residues throughout CaM upon H1 binding at 1:2 stoichiometry, highlighting binding of H1 to both lobes.
source: Large CSPs were observed for residues throughout CaM, highlighting binding of H1 to both lobes.
evidence: Supported by NMR chemical shift perturbation data.

claim: The rate constants for dissociation of H1 from the C-lobe and N-lobe were determined by 2D NMR lineshape analysis to koff,1 = 40 ± 5 s−1 and koff,2 = 16 ± 3 s−1, respectively.
source: The rate constants for dissociation of H1 from the C-lobe and N-lobe were determined by 2D NMR lineshape analysis to koff,1 = 40 ± 5 s−1 and koff,2 = 16 ± 3 s−1, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, Table 2), revealing a >10 times faster association with the C-lobe than with the N-lobe.
evidence: Supported by NMR lineshape analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and Table 2.

claim: At a 1:2 (CaM:H1) molar ratio, two sets of signals from 15N-labeled H1 became distinct and could be assigned to H1 bound to either of the two CaM lobes, respectively.
source: Only a few signals from the free peptide were visible at 37°C, presumably due to its disordered nature, while at a 1:2 (CaM:H1) molar ratio, two sets of signals became distinct and could be assigned to H1 bound to either of the two CaM lobes, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: When more CaM was added to 15N-labeled H1 (at 3:1 CaM:H1 ratio), the set of signals originating from H1 bound to the N-lobe decreased in intensity and vanished, with the peptide almost exclusively bound to the higher affinity C-lobe of CaM.
source: When more CaM was added, the set of signals originating from H1 bound to the N-lobe decreased in intensity and vanished at a molar ratio of 3:1 (CaM:H1). At this condition, the peptide was almost exclusively bound to the higher affinity C-lobe of CaM (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Titration of H2 into 15N-labeled CaM showed NMR signals gradually moving with increasing peptide concentration, indicating the free and bound states to be in fast exchange on the NMR timescale.
source: We next titrated 15N-labeled CaM with the low-affinity H2 peptide. Here, in contrast to the H1 titration, the NMR signals were gradually moving with increasing peptide concentration, indicating the free and bound states to be in fast exchange on the NMR timescale (kex > Δδ, Figure 2e–f, Prestel et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2e–f and citation to NMR methodology.

claim: 2D NMR lineshape analysis of H2:CaM interaction resulted in affinity and dissociation rate constants of Kd = 16 ± 1 µM and koff = 2600 ± 100 s−1, respectively.
source: The change in peak position could be followed throughout the titration, and 2D NMR lineshape analysis resulted in affinity and dissociation rate constants of Kd = 16 ± 1 µM and koff = 2600 ± 100 s−1, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b, Table 2).
evidence: Supported by NMR lineshape analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and Table 2.

claim: Chemical shift perturbations induced by H2 binding spanned both CaM lobes, although they were less pronounced for the C-lobe and generally smaller compared to those induced by H1 binding.
source: Again, the CSPs spanned both CaM lobes (Figure 2h), although they were less pronounced for the C-lobe and generally smaller compared to those induced by H1 binding.
evidence: Supported by NMR chemical shift perturbation data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: Each of the CaM lobes can bind one NHE1 H1 with high affinity forming a 1:2 complex, with the C-lobe energetically slightly favored.
source: Taken together, these data show that each of the CaM lobes can bind one NHE1 H1 with high affinity forming a 1:2 complex, with the C-lobe energetically slightly favored.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from NMR and ITC data.

claim: CaM binds NHE1 H2 with lower affinity in a 1:1 complex with both CaM lobes involved.
source: CaM binds NHE1 H2 with lower affinity in a 1:1 complex with both CaM lobes involved, suggesting a more classical CaM binding as depicted in the cartoon in Figure 2g.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from NMR and ITC data, depicted in Figure 2g.

claim: At a molar ratio of 1:2 (CaM:H1H2), the 15N HSQC spectrum closely resembled the state where only H1 is present in twofold excess.
source: At a molar ratio of 1:2 (CaM:H1H2), the 15N HSQC spectrum closely resembled the state where only H1 is present in twofold excess (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3a–c.

claim: At 1:2 stoichiometry (CaM:H1H2), each CaM lobe interacts with one H1 of H1H2 in a ternary complex, while H2 is not involved in the interaction.
source: This suggested that at this stoichiometry each CaM lobe interacts with one H1 of H1H2 in a ternary complex, while H2 is not involved in the interaction, as depicted in Figure 3a.
evidence: Inferred from NMR data and depicted in Figure 3a.

claim: At a stoichiometry of 1:1 (CaM:H1H2), the signals of the N-lobe of CaM overlaid with the spectrum of CaM at saturation with H1, while signals of the C-lobe overlaid with the spectrum of CaM bound to H2.
source: At a stoichiometry of 1:1, the signals of the N-lobe of CaM still overlaid almost perfectly with the spectrum of 15N-labeled CaM at saturation with H1. However, signals of the C-lobe now overlaid with the spectrum of CaM bound to H2 (Figure 3d–f).
evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3d–f.

claim: At 1:1 molar ratio (CaM:H1H2), the major state is the N-lobe of CaM bound to H1 and the C-lobe bound to H2.
source: Thus, at this molar ratio, the major state is the N-lobe of CaM bound to H1 and the C-lobe bound to H2, as depicted in Figure 3d.
evidence: Inferred from NMR data and depicted in Figure 3d.

claim: A second set of very weak NMR peaks was detectable for many residues at 1:1 (CaM:H1H2) stoichiometry, suggesting the presence of a minor state with the opposite architecture: the N-lobe of CaM bound to H2 and the C-lobe bound to H1.
source: It is worth noting that a second set of very weak peaks was detectable for many of the residues. Comparing these to the spectra from the simpler systems of the individual peptides, this suggested the presence of a minor state with the opposite architecture: the N-lobe of CaM bound to H2 and the C-lobe bound to H1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The severely broadened NMR signals at 1:1 (CaM:H1H2) stoichiometry may be explained by exchange between two states, with the equilibrium highly shifted toward the H1:N-lobe;H2:C-lobe complex.
source: The severely broadened signals may thus be explained by exchange between these two states, and judging from the relative signal intensities, the equilibrium was highly shifted toward the H1:N-lobe;H2:C-lobe complex, as depicted in Figure 3d.
evidence: Inferred from NMR data and depicted in Figure 3d.

claim: At a stoichiometry of 1:2 (CaM:H1H2), two sets of signals originated from each residue of H1 in 15N-labeled H1H2, while signals from H2 closely resembled those of unbound H2.
source: At a stoichiometry of 1:2 (CaM:H1H2), two sets of signals originated from each residue of H1, while signals from H2 closely resembled those of unbound H2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claim: At a stoichiometry of 1:1 (CaM:H1H2), signals from H1 in 15N-labeled H1H2 overlapped with the N-lobe bound state, while signals from H2 were either invisible or closely resembled the C-lobe bound state.
source: At a stoichiometry of 1:1, signals from H1 overlapped with the N-lobe bound state, while signals from H2 were either invisible or closely resembled the C-lobe bound state (Figure 2—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2d.

claim: At 1:1 and 1:2 (CaM:H1H2) stoichiometries, the NMR signals were drastically broadened compared to those of free CaM or of the 1:2 complex saturated with H1, indicating a dynamic equilibrium of states with different stoichiometries.
source: It is, however, important to note that at 1:1 as well as 1:2 (CaM:H1H2) stoichiometries the NMR signals were drastically broadened compared to those of free CaM or of the 1:2 complex saturated with H1 (Figure 3a, d), indicating a dynamic equilibrium of states with different stoichiometries, including potential higher order oligomers.
evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3a, d.

claim: The mass of the CaM:H1H2 complex at a 1:1 stoichiometry as determined from SEC-MALS (25.0 ± 1.6 kDa) was in perfect agreement with the expected molecular weight of a 1:1 complex (25.5 kDa).
source: The mass of the complex at a 1:1 stoichiometry as determined from SEC-MALS (25.0 ± 1.6 kDa) was in perfect agreement with the expected molecular weight of a 1:1 complex (25.5 kDa) and suggested that, if higher oligomers were present, their population was low under these conditions.
evidence: Supported by SEC-MALS data.

claim: DLS and PFG-NMR showed a stepwise increase of the complex size from free CaM to the complexes formed at 1:1 and 1:2 stoichiometries, respectively.
source: However, these complexes were readily accessible by DLS and PFG-NMR: both experiment series showed a stepwise increase of the complex size from free CaM to the complexes formed at 1:1 and 1:2 stoichiometries, respectively.
evidence: Supported by DLS and PFG-NMR data.

claim: The NMR solution structure of the ternary complex shows that both CaM lobes have one H1 bound inside the hydrophobic cleft.
source: Both CaM lobes have one H1 bound inside the hydrophobic cleft (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by NMR structure shown in Figure 4a.

claim: An overlay of the 10 lowest energy structures shows that the individual lobes are well defined (backbone RMSD: N-lobe + H1N = 0.77 ± 0.16 Å; backbone RMSD C-lobe + H1c = 0.83 ± 0.18 Å), while no NOEs between the two lobes could be obtained, suggesting that the linker region remains flexible in the bound state.
source: An overlay of the 10 lowest energy structures shows that the individual lobes are well defined (backbone RMSD: N-lobe + H1N = 0.77 ± 0.16 Å; backbone RMSD C-lobe + H1c = 0.83 ± 0.18 Å), while no NOEs between the two lobes could be obtained, suggesting that the linker region remains flexible in the bound state (Figure 4b, c).
evidence: Supported by NMR structure data shown in Figure 4b, c.

claim: In both lobes, the interaction surface is defined by contacts between the hydrophobic face of the amphipathic H1 (L623, I631, I634, L635, N638, L639, T642, and L646) and the central methionines in the hydrophobic cleft of each CaM-lobe.
source: In both lobes, the interaction surface is defined by contacts between the hydrophobic face of the amphipathic H1 (L623, I631, I634, L635, N638, L639, T642, and L646; Figure 4d, e) and the central methionines in the hydrophobic cleft of each CaM-lobe.
evidence: Supported by NMR structure data shown in Figure 4d, e.

claim: For the N-lobe, the interaction involves M37, M52, M72, and M73; and for the C-lobe M110, M125, M145, and M146.
source: For the N-lobe, this involves M37, M52, M72, and M73; and for the C-lobe M110, M125, M145, and M146.
evidence: Supported by NMR structure data.

claim: A high complementarity in electrostatics is evident, with multiple positively charged residues on the opposite side of NHE1 H1 (K625, K637, R632, K633, R636, K641, R643, R645) complementing the negatively charged surface of CaM.
source: In addition, a high complementarity in electrostatics is evident, with multiple positively charged residues on the opposite side of NHE1 H1 (K625, K637, R632, K633, R636, K641, R643, R645) complementing the negatively charged surface of CaM (Figure 4f–i).
evidence: Supported by NMR structure data shown in Figure 4f–i.

claim: The mode of interaction between the CaM C-lobe and H1 described by NMR was also present in the crystal structure, but was translated as crystal contacts between symmetry-related molecules.
source: Although this complex is very different from that shown in the published crystal structure (Köster et al., 2011), inspection of the neighboring molecules in the crystal lattice reveals that the mode of interaction between the CaM C-lobe and H1, which we describe here by NMR, was also present in the crystal, but was translated as crystal contacts between symmetry-related molecules (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of NMR structure with crystal structure shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the absence of Ca2+, chemical shift perturbations and line broadening of apo-CaM were observable after addition of excess NHE1 H1H2, showing that NHE1:CaM complex formation can also occur in the absence of Ca2+.
source: In the absence of Ca2+, we still observed CSPs of CaM after addition of 2.5-fold molar excess of H1H2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a), suggesting that also the Ca2+-free form of CaM binds NHE1 H1H2.
evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Under conditions where both Ca2+ and high EDTA were present, in the additional presence of 2.5-fold molar excess of H1H2, signals of the C-lobe overlapped with those from Ca2+-CaM bound to H1, while signals of the N-lobe closely resembled the Ca2+-free state.
source: Under conditions where both Ca2+ (here 2 mM) and high EDTA (here 6.6 mM) were present, free CaM gets stripped of Ca2+. However, in the additional presence of 2.5-fold molar excess of H1H2, signals of the C-lobe overlapped with those from Ca2+-CaM bound to H1, while signals of the N-lobe closely resembled the Ca2+-free state (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The presence of H1 increased the affinity for Ca2+ in the C-lobe of CaM.
source: Thus, the presence of H1 increased the affinity for Ca2+ in the C-lobe.
evidence: Inferred from NMR data showing Ca2+ binding to C-lobe in presence of H1 under Ca2+-limiting conditions.

claim: S648 is located at the C-terminal distal end of H1.
source: S648, which can be phosphorylated by Akt (Meima et al., 2009; Snabaitis et al., 2008), is located at the C-terminal distal end of H1.
evidence: Describes the location of S648 based on sequence and structural information.

claim: In cardiomyocytes, the S648A mutation increased CaM binding to NHE1 in vitro, and S648 phosphorylation by Akt was proposed to inhibit NHE1 by preventing CaM binding.
source: In cardiomyocytes, the S648A mutation increased CaM binding to NHE1 in vitro, and S648 phosphorylation by Akt was proposed to inhibit NHE1 by preventing CaM binding (Snabaitis et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study in cardiomyocytes.

claim: In fibroblasts, S648 phosphorylation by Akt was required for NHE1 activation by platelet-derived growth factor.
source: In contrast, in fibroblasts, S648 phosphorylation by Akt was required for NHE1 activation by platelet-derived growth factor (Meima et al., 2009), indicating that the impact of this residue may be cell-type- and/or context-specific.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study in fibroblasts.

claim: WT NHE1 and all three variants (H1-CR, S648A, S648D) localized primarily to the plasma membrane in PS120 cells.
source: WT NHE1 and all three variants localized primarily to the plasma membrane – the expected pattern for exogenously expressed NHE1 localization in PS120 cells (Figure 5; Denker and Barber, 2002; Hendus-Altenburger et al., 2016; Hendus-Altenburger et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5 and citations to prior studies.

claim: NHE1 protein expression levels were comparable between cell lines, albeit slightly higher in cells expressing the variants compared to WT.
source: NHE1 protein expression levels were comparable between cell lines, albeit slightly higher in cells expressing the variants compared to WT, as shown by immunoblot analysis (Figure 5b, c).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5b, c.

claim: Endogenous CaM exhibited similar expression levels in all cell lines.
source: As expected, endogenous CaM exhibited similar expression levels in all cell lines (Figure 5b, d) and localized mainly diffusely in the cytosol (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5b, d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The steady-state pHi was similar between all cell lines, ranging from ~7.4 to 7.5.
source: The steady-state pHi was similar between all cell lines, ranging from ~7.4 to 7.5 (Figure 5e).
evidence: Supported by pHi measurement data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Following an acid load without further stimulation, recovery rates were not significantly different between cells expressing WT and variant NHE1s.
source: Following an acid load without further stimulation, recovery rates were not significantly different between cells expressing WT and variant NHE1s (Figure 5f, g).
evidence: Supported by pHi recovery data shown in Figure 5f, g.

claim: In the presence of ionomycin, cells expressing WT NHE1 recovered significantly faster than WT vehicle controls.
source: In the presence of the Ca2+-ionophore ionomycin, which causes elevated [Ca2+]i, added concomitantly with the acid load, cells expressing WT NHE1 recovered significantly faster than WT vehicle controls (Figure 5h, i), in agreement with previous reports (Wakabayashi et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by pHi recovery data shown in Figure 5h, i and citation to prior study.

claim: Under ionomycin-stimulated conditions, recovery was significantly reduced in cells expressing the NHE1 H1-CR and S648D variants compared to those expressing WT NHE1.
source: Under ionomycin-stimulated conditions, recovery was significantly reduced in cells expressing the NHE1 H1-CR and S648D variants compared to those expressing WT NHE1 (Figure 5h, i).
evidence: Supported by pHi recovery data shown in Figure 5h, i.

claim: PLA puncta representing ≤40 nM proximity of CaM and NHE1 were clearly detected in PS120 cells expressing WT NHE1.
source: In PS120 cells expressing WT NHE1, PLA puncta, representing ≤40 nM proximity of CaM and NHE1, were clearly detected (Figure 6a, b).
evidence: Supported by PLA data shown in Figure 6a, b.

claim: The number of PLA puncta per area did not increase upon ionomycin treatment.
source: The number of PLA puncta per area did not increase upon ionomycin treatment (Figure 6a, b), suggesting that an increase in [Ca2+]i does not detectably increase the number of CaM and NHE1 proteins within close proximity of each other.
evidence: Supported by PLA data shown in Figure 6a, b.

claim: None of the three variants (H1-CR, S648A, S648D) abolished NHE1:CaM PLA in situ.
source: In contrast to their inhibitory effect on Ca2+-induced NHE1 activation (Figure 5h, i), none of the three variants abolished NHE1:CaM PLA in situ (Figure 6a, b).
evidence: Supported by PLA data shown in Figure 6a, b.

claim: In the NMR solution structure of the 1:2 (CaM:H1) complex, the four residues K641, R643, R645, and R648 are all solvent exposed both when bound to the N-lobe or the C-lobe of CaM.
source: In the complex, the four residues K641, R643, R645, and R648 are all solvent exposed both when bound to the N-lobe or the C-lobe of CaM, with some hydrophobic contacts from K641 (Figure 6c, d).
evidence: Supported by NMR structure data shown in Figure 6c, d.

claim: In either of the lobes, S648 does not form direct contacts with CaM.
source: Likewise, in either of the lobes, S648 does not form direct contacts with CaM (Figure 6c, d).
evidence: Supported by NMR structure data shown in Figure 6c, d.

claim: Phosphorylation of a single residue by Akt was confirmed by mass spectrometry, and S648 was identified by NMR.
source: Phosphorylation of a single residue by Akt was confirmed by mass spectrometry, and S648 was identified by NMR, while PKCδ gave rise to mono-, double-, and triple phosphorylated forms of H1H2, identified by NMR at residues T642, S648, and T653 (Figure 6h, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry and NMR data shown in Figure 6h and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: PKCδ gave rise to mono-, double-, and triple phosphorylated forms of H1H2, identified by NMR at residues T642, S648, and T653.
source: Phosphorylation of a single residue by Akt was confirmed by mass spectrometry, and S648 was identified by NMR, while PKCδ gave rise to mono-, double-, and triple phosphorylated forms of H1H2, identified by NMR at residues T642, S648, and T653 (Figure 6h, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry and NMR data shown in Figure 6h and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Phosphorylation of S648 results in a tenfold weakened binding to CaM compared to WT (Kd,1 = 5 ± 4 nM for first binding event, Kd,2 = 2700 ± 600 nM for second binding event).
source: The first binding event gave a Kd,1 = 5 ± 4 nM with a stoichiometry n1 = 0.93 ± 0.02, while the second binding event gave a Kd,1 = 2700 ± 600 nM with n2 = 1.16 ± 0.06 (Figure 6i, Table 1). Thus, indeed, phosphorylation of S648 results in a tenfold weakened binding to CaM compared to WT.
evidence: Supported by ITC data shown in Figure 6i and Table 1.

claim: A 10 min stimulation with ionomycin had no detectable effect on Akt activation (phosphorylation) in PS120 cells.
source: A 10 min stimulation with ionomycin had no detectable effect on Akt activation (phosphorylation) in PS120 cells (Figure 6g).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6g.

claim: Akt activity was ablated under both control and ionomycin conditions by the Akt inhibitor Akti-1/2.
source: Furthermore, Akt activity was ablated under both control and ionomycin conditions by the Akt inhibitor Akti-1/2 (Figure 6g), yet Akti-1/2 had no significant effect on ionomycin-stimulated NHE1 activity after an acid load (Figure 6e).
evidence: Supported by western blot and pHi recovery data shown in Figure 6g and Figure 6e.

claim: Akti-1/2 had no significant effect on ionomycin-stimulated NHE1 activity after an acid load.
source: Furthermore, Akt activity was ablated under both control and ionomycin conditions by the Akt inhibitor Akti-1/2 (Figure 6g), yet Akti-1/2 had no significant effect on ionomycin-stimulated NHE1 activity after an acid load (Figure 6e).
evidence: Supported by pHi recovery data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Two PKC inhibitors, bisindolylmaleimide I (BIM I) and Gö6983, had no significant effects on the Ca2+-dependent NHE1 activity after acidification.
source: Similarly, two well-established PKC inhibitors, bisindolylmaleimide I (BIM I) – targeting PKCα, -β1, -β2, -γ, -δ, and -ε – and Gö6983 – targeting PKCα, PKCβ, -γ, -δ, and -ζ (Figure 6f) – also had no significant effects on the Ca2+-dependent NHE1 activity after acidification.
evidence: Supported by pHi recovery data shown in Figure 6f.

claim: In solution, NHE1 and CaM can form either 1:1 or 2:1 (NHE1:CaM) complexes with similar affinities but different structures.
source: In vitro, we found that NHE1 and CaM can form either 1:1 or 2:1 (NHE1:CaM) complexes with similar affinities but different structures, suggesting that the complex is highly dynamic and that the relevant state at any time is dependent on the availability of Ca2+-CaM and NHE1 in the cell (Figure 7).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from NMR and ITC data, depicted in Figure 7.

claim: In the absence of Ca2+, apo-CaM can associate weakly with NHE1-binding sites in a different type of complex.
source: In the absence of Ca2+, apo-CaM can associate weakly with NHE1-binding sites in a different type of complex (Figure 7c).
evidence: Supported by NMR data and depicted in Figure 7c.

claim: At low Ca2+ levels, NHE1:CaM interaction can stabilize Ca2+-binding to the C-lobe of CaM, resulting in an apo-state N-lobe and a Ca2+-loaded C-lobe bound to H1.
source: Under such low Ca2+ conditions, our results show that in vitro NHE1:CaM interaction can stabilize Ca2+-binding to the C-lobe of CaM, resulting in an apo-state N-lobe and a Ca2+-loaded C-lobe bound to H1 (Figure 7d).
evidence: Supported by NMR data and depicted in Figure 7d.

claim: At higher [Ca2+-CaM], two scenarios are possible: one is a 1:1 NHE1:CaM complex, with the major state having the N-lobe bound to H1 and the C-lobe bound to H2.
source: At higher [Ca2+-CaM], corresponding to, for example, mitogenic stimuli, which can increase [Ca2+]i to up to around 1 µM, the present study indicates that two scenarios are possible: one is a 1:1 NHE1:CaM complex, with the major state having the N-lobe bound to H1 and the C-lobe bound to H2 (Figure 7e), and the second is a 2:1 NHE1:CaM complex, with the CaM N- and C-lobes both interacting with H1 on two adjacent NHE1 C-tails, potentially stabilizing the dimeric state of NHE1 (Figure 7f).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from NMR data and depicted in Figure 7e.

claim: At higher [Ca2+-CaM], the second scenario is a 2:1 NHE1:CaM complex, with the CaM N- and C-lobes both interacting with H1 on two adjacent NHE1 C-tails, potentially stabilizing the dimeric state of NHE1.
source: At higher [Ca2+-CaM], corresponding to, for example, mitogenic stimuli, which can increase [Ca2+]i to up to around 1 µM, the present study indicates that two scenarios are possible: one is a 1:1 NHE1:CaM complex, with the major state having the N-lobe bound to H1 and the C-lobe bound to H2 (Figure 7e), and the second is a 2:1 NHE1:CaM complex, with the CaM N- and C-lobes both interacting with H1 on two adjacent NHE1 C-tails, potentially stabilizing the dimeric state of NHE1 (Figure 7f).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from NMR data and depicted in Figure 7f.

claim: The total cellular [CaM] is 5–6 µM as measured in various cell types.
source: Although the total cellular [CaM] is 5–6 µM as measured in various cell types, the global free Ca2+-CaM concentration in a cell has been estimated to be around 50 nM, that is, ~1% of the total [CaM] (Persechini and Stemmer, 2002; Saucerman and Bers, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies measuring cellular CaM concentrations.

claim: The global free Ca2+-CaM concentration in a cell has been estimated to be around 50 nM, that is, ~1% of the total [CaM].
source: Although the total cellular [CaM] is 5–6 µM as measured in various cell types, the global free Ca2+-CaM concentration in a cell has been estimated to be around 50 nM, that is, ~1% of the total [CaM] (Persechini and Stemmer, 2002; Saucerman and Bers, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies estimating free Ca2+-CaM concentrations.

claim: CaM-mediated oligomerization has been reported for both soluble and membrane proteins.
source: CaM-mediated oligomerization has been reported for both soluble and membrane proteins.
evidence: Refers to established knowledge about CaM-mediated oligomerization.

claim: Two ERα bind to one Ca2+-CaM, one in each lobe, to maximally activate transcription.
source: Examples of the former include the ERα, with two ERα binding to one Ca2+-CaM, one in each lobe, to maximally activate transcription (Li et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies of ERα-CaM interaction.

claim: The affinity of one CaM lobe for ERα is almost 100-fold lower than what we measured for H1 of NHE1.
source: The affinity of one CaM lobe for ERα is almost 100-fold lower than what we measured for H1 of NHE1, further supporting a unique role of the 1:2 CaM:NHE1 complex.
evidence: Comparison of measured affinities with literature values.

claim: For SK channel monomers, 1:1 complexes with apo-CaM form through C-lobe binding, keeping the channel inactive; when [Ca2+]i increases, the N-lobe also associates with the channel, triggering dimerization and channel opening.
source: Small-conductance Ca2+-activated K+-(SK) channel monomers form 1:1 complexes with apo-CaM through C-lobe binding, thereby keeping the channel inactive. When [Ca2+]i increases, the N-lobe also associates with the channel, triggering dimerization and channel opening (Barros et al., 2019; Lee and MacKinnon, 2018; Schumacher et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies of SK channel-CaM interaction.

claim: For the eag1/Kv10.1 channel, the stoichiometry is 1:1, and it is proposed that CaM acts as a molecular clamp interacting with domains from neighboring subunits, thereby 'twisting' the pore closed.
source: Another example is the eag1/Kv10.1 channel, which is inhibited by CaM. Also for this interaction, the stoichiometry is 1:1, and it is proposed that CaM acts as a molecular clamp interacting with domains from neighboring subunits, thereby 'twisting' the pore closed (Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to study of eag1/Kv10.1 channel-CaM interaction.

claim: CaM binding may contribute to NHE1 C-tail dimerization in a 2:1 (NHE1:CaM) stoichiometry.
source: Based on our findings, it could be speculated that CaM binding contributes to NHE1 C-tail dimerization in a similar way as was observed for ERα, with CaM binding to H1 on two separate NHE1s in a 2:1 (NHE1:CaM) stoichiometry (Figure 7f), as shown in the ternary complex (Figure 4).
evidence: Speculation based on NMR structure data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 7f.

claim: A role for CaM as a dimerization switch would provide a structural understanding of previous reports of dimerization sites in the C-terminal tail of NHE1.
source: However, a role for CaM as a dimerization switch would provide a structural understanding of previous reports of dimerization sites in the C-terminal tail of NHE1 (Fafournoux et al., 1994; Hisamitsu et al., 2004), as well as reports based on kinetic analyses of transport indicating that dimerization contributes to the regulation of NHE1 activity (Fuster et al., 2008; Hisamitsu et al., 2006; Lacroix et al., 2004; Otsu et al., 1989).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to prior studies on NHE1 dimerization.

claim: Ca2+-CaM could regulate NHE1 through electrostatic tuning of the NHE1:PI(4,5)P2 interaction.
source: Finally, given the key role of anionic lipids including phosphatidyl-inositol(4,5)-diphosphate (PI[4,5]P2) in regulating NHE1 by interacting with the C-tail (Aharonovitz et al., 2000; Shimada-Shimizu et al., 2014), Ca2+-CaM could also regulate NHE1 through electrostatic tuning of the NHE1:PI(4,5)P2 interaction. Such mechanisms are reported for several other membrane proteins (Cao et al., 2013; Monteiro et al., 2014) and would be consistent with the folding of the NHE1-LID domain upon membrane interaction, bringing the CaM-binding region in close proximity to the NHE1-LID and the membrane (Hendus-Altenburger et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to studies on lipid regulation and membrane protein mechanisms.

claim: The effect of phosphorylation on the NHE1:CaM interaction was not strong enough to fully prevent interaction in vivo.
source: This may reflect that the effect of phosphorylation on the interaction was not strong enough to fully prevent interaction in vivo.
evidence: Speculation to explain PLA results.

claim: Cellular NHE1:CaM interactions may occur through C-tail interactions with other proteins (e.g., calcineurin) or membrane lipids, independent of the residues studied here but also giving rise to PLA signals.
source: Additionally, cellular NHE1:CaM interactions may occur through C-tail interactions with other proteins (e.g., calcineurin) or membrane lipids (Hendus-Altenburger et al., 2019; Hendus-Altenburger et al., 2020), independent of the residues studied here but also giving rise to PLA signals.
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to prior studies on NHE1 interactions.

claim: The observed binding of NHE1 to apo-CaM in vitro and the lack of effect of ionomycin on the number of proximity events observed in cells indicate that a fraction of NHE1:CaM complexes are present at all times.
source: Finally, while NHE1:CaM proximity in the absence of interaction cannot be excluded, the observed binding of NHE1 to apo-CaM in vitro and the lack of effect of ionomycin on the number of proximity events observed in cells indicate that a fraction of NHE1:CaM complexes are present at all times.
evidence: Inference drawn from NMR and PLA data.

claim: S648 was phosphorylated in vitro by both Akt and PKC, which have overlapping consensus sites, strongly indicating that other kinases than Akt can act via S648 to regulate NHE1.
source: Furthermore, S648 was phosphorylated in vitro by both Akt and PKC, which have overlapping consensus sites, strongly indicating that other kinases than Akt can act via S648 to regulate NHE1.
evidence: Inference drawn from in vitro phosphorylation data.

claim: T653 has been implicated in NHE1 regulation by Rho kinase and β-Raf.
source: T653 has not been studied in the context of CaM but has been implicated in NHE1 regulation by Rho kinase (Wallert et al., 2015) and β-Raf (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on T653 phosphorylation.

claim: We show that NHE1 and CaM engage in diverse complexes of different NHE1:CaM stoichiometries and structures in vitro.
source: In conclusion, we show that NHE1 and CaM engage in diverse complexes of different NHE1:CaM stoichiometries and structures in vitro.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from NMR and ITC data.

claim: The interactions can be dynamically tuned by variations in the concentrations of NHE1, CaM, and Ca2+ and by phosphorylation of S648.
source: The interactions can be dynamically tuned by variations in the concentrations of NHE1, CaM, and Ca2+ and by phosphorylation of S648.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from NMR, ITC, and phosphorylation data.

claim: In cells, Ca2+-induced NHE1 activity was reduced by mutation in the first CaM-binding helix, as well as by mimicking S648 phosphorylation, but not by inhibition of Akt.
source: In cells, Ca2+-induced NHE1 activity was reduced by mutation in the first CaM-binding helix, as well as by mimicking S648 phosphorylation, but not by inhibition of Akt.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from pHi recovery data.

claim: NHE1:CaM proximity was not lost by H1-CR, S648A, or S648D mutations, likely reflecting further complexity of NHE1:CaM interactions in vivo.
source: In contrast, NHE1:CaM proximity was not lost by these mutations, likely reflecting further complexity of NHE1:CaM interactions in vivo.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from PLA data.

claim: S648 phosphorylation in vitro was facilitated by both Akt and PKC, and Ca2+-stimulated NHE1 activity was not affected by Akt inhibition, suggesting that multiple kinases regulate S648 phosphorylation in vivo.
source: S648 phosphorylation in vitro was facilitated by both Akt and PKC, and Ca2+-stimulated NHE1 activity was not affected by Akt inhibition, suggesting that multiple kinases regulate S648 phosphorylation in vivo.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from phosphorylation and pHi recovery data.

claim: We determined the structure of the ternary complex between CaM and two NHE1 peptides, pointing to a possible role of CaM in stabilizing NHE1 dimers via binding to two C-terminal regulatory tails.
source: Finally, we determined the structure of the ternary complex between CaM and two NHE1 peptides, pointing to a possible role of CaM in stabilizing NHE1 dimers via binding to two C-terminal regulatory tails.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from NMR structure data.

claim: An additional NHE1 regulatory layer tuned by Ca2+-CaM availability may contribute to NHE1 dimerization.
source: Our results provide novel insight into the dynamics and regulation of NHE1:CaM interaction, and we suggest that an additional NHE1 regulatory layer tuned by Ca2+-CaM availability may contribute to NHE1 dimerization.
evidence: Summary conclusion and speculation based on all data.

claim: Similar regulatory mechanisms and structural diversity may be relevant for tuning oligomerization and function in many other membrane proteins.
source: As CaM binding to membrane proteins is widespread, similar regulatory mechanisms and structural diversity may be relevant for tuning oligomerization and function in many other membrane proteins.
evidence: Speculation about broader implications of findings.
